## Statistical hypotheses and severe testing {#testing}

For quantitative work, the particular hypotheses of the previous section must be turned into **statistical hypotheses**: expectations about a numerical outcome of counting or measuring. Given the low degree of formalisation, that outcome is usually as imprecise as "$n$ should be greater than $m$." For the loss of number marking on pre-nominal elements under Norse contact, for instance, we might expect inflected pre-nominal elements to occur less often in Northern and Eastern dialects than in Southern and Western ones during the Danelaw. Call this $H_1$: "*Occurrence counts of inflected pre-nominal elements are lower in the North and East than in the South and West.*"

Now comes the moment of truth. It is statistically far easier to check a sample for *divergence* from a hypothesis than for *accordance* with it, so the hypothesis is inverted into a *Null*, $H_0$, and frequentist theory gives the probability of obtaining a sample at least as extreme as the observed one if the Null were true --- the p-value. A low p-value is then usually read as licence to infer $H_1$.

That inference has been under heavy fire for two decades, almost unnoticed in linguistics.^[A marginal but real debate about significance testing in corpus linguistics does exist [@Kilgarriff2005; @Koplenig2019].] It is typically made through Null-Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST): the p-value falls below a threshold (often 0.05), and this is treated as straightforward corroboration of $H_1$ --- more often than not an incorrect inference [@Gigerenzer2004; @GreenlandEa2016; @Mayo2018]. Part of the trouble is that NHST is an unstable hybrid of two incompatible inferential philosophies, Fisher's significance testing and the Neyman--Pearson theory of decisions between hypotheses, welded into a procedure neither founder would endorse.

Mayo's *severity* requirement makes the deeper problem precise [@Mayo1996; @MayoSpanos2004; @Mayo2018]. In its weak form: *data do not provide good evidence for a hypothesis if they come from a procedure with very little capacity to have detected the hypothesis's falsity, had it been false* [paraphrased from @MayoSpanos2004, 162]. A hypothesis earns the label *corroborated* only by surviving tests with a real chance of exposing it. Reading a single low p-value, derived from one Null, as corroboration of the whole network of substantive and particular hypotheses behind it (Section \@ref(hypotheses)) is a flagrant breach of that requirement: such a test has almost no capacity to detect error in the hypotheses that actually matter.

The crucial point is that *any* real divergence, however slight, makes the Null false --- and NHST detects it as a low p-value. Suppose the effect posited in Study 1 held for one ten-thousandth of speakers. The Null would then be technically false, NHST would flag it given a large enough sample (or simply an unlucky one containing a text or two from those few speakers), and the result could be paraded as corroboration of Trudgill's theory. It would be nothing of the kind: no severe test was performed, and a discrepancy that small tells us nothing about English under the Danelaw. This is also the mechanism behind the loose fit of Section \@ref(hypotheses): a low-severity test is precisely how an informal, underdetermined theory manufactures the "confirmation" we argued it could never legitimately earn. The fault is not in frequentist inference but in this use of it.

Many of the deficiencies we document below stem from this adherence to NHST. We will argue in Section \@ref(gooduse) that a few straightforward practices --- careful, bias-resistant inspection of one's own models; reviewers equipped to catch statistical error; and relief from the pressure to report only positive findings --- would have forestalled most of them. We do not suspect the authors of dredging or negligence; we are confident they acted in good faith, having seen the same confusions in many other researchers and in our own earlier work. But the field suffers if papers like @WalkdenEa2023 pass without methodological scrutiny.
